native_result.query: Does increased time preference leads to higher BMI?
native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: Higher time preference (present-orientation/impatience) is associated with significantly higher BMI in early adulthood: 1989 savers (put more money into savings, the lowest time-preference group) had BMI in 1992 about 0.4–0.5 units lower (≈0.08 SD) and 38–90% lower odds of obesity than dis-savers/non-savers, after adjustment for SES, education, race/ethnicity, sex, age, family background, cognitive ability and baseline BMI. The pattern is consistent with a causal role of time preference but is an observational association, not proof of causation.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Unit forensics: heights 1981 decoded from feet+inches; weights confirmed as pounds though codebook says kg (validated by BMI plausibility). 2) BMI outcomes built for 1981/1989/1992 (703*lbs/in^2), implausible values excluded. 3) Time-preference proxies: primary = 1989 savings direction (put_in/took_out/no_change/no_savings) with impatient-vs-patient and saver-vs-not contrasts; secondary = wealth-for-income residual, jailed/incarceration indicators; composite as robustness. 4) OLS/GLM models: bivariate and fully-adjusted (sex, race, age89, education, log income89, parental education, family size, ASVAB, sampling stratum, baseline BMI81); outcomes BMI 1992 (primary), BMI 1989, ΔBMI 1981-92, obesity>=30 (secondary). 5) Missingness/attrition reported at each sample; analytic vs full-file comparisons on observables. 6) Sign-consistency across 8 proxy variants assessed before wording.

sub_hypo.text: Higher time preference is associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
sub_hypo.context: Participants in the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth (NLSY79), using 1989 data and height measured in 1985.
variables: Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989: time preference proxy, encoded as DISSAVED = 1 for 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' and 0 otherwise; SAMESAVE = 1 for 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' and 0 otherwise
BMI: derived from Weight of respondent, 1989 and Height of respondent, 1985
sub_hypo.relations: Positive association between time preference and BMI, tested using OLS regression with DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as the dependent variable.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.

sub_hypo.text: Higher time preference (present-orientation or impatience), primarily proxied by 1989 savings direction, is associated with significantly higher BMI in early adulthood. Savers had BMI in 1992 about 0.4–0.5 units lower (approximately 0.08 SD) and 38–90% lower odds of obesity than dis-savers/non-savers after adjustment. This observational pattern is consistent with, but does not establish, a causal role of time preference.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 participants in early adulthood with usable savings, BMI and adjustment data; 1989 savings behavior predicts primarily 1992 BMI and obesity, with implausible BMI values excluded.
variables: Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989
Derived BMI in 1981, 1989 and 1992 (703 × weight in pounds / height in inches squared)
Age of respondent at interview date, 1989
Total net family income, previous calendar year, 1989 (log-transformed)
Highest grade completed by respondent's mother, 1979
Highest grade completed by respondent's father, 1979
sub_hypo.relations: Positive adjusted association between time preference and BMI/obesity: putting more money into savings in 1989 identifies the lowest-time-preference group, whose 1992 BMI was approximately 0.4–0.5 units (0.08 SD) lower and whose obesity odds were 38–90% lower than those of dis-savers/non-savers. OLS/GLM analyses adjust for sex, race/ethnicity, age in 1989, education, log income in 1989, parental education, family size, ASVAB cognitive ability, sampling stratum and baseline BMI in 1981. Secondary outcomes are BMI in 1989 and BMI change from 1981 to 1992; no separate effect sizes are specified for these outcomes. The relationship is observational, not proof of causation.

gen_sub_hypo.full_hypo: Higher time preference (present-orientation/impatience) is associated with significantly higher BMI in early adulthood: 1989 savers (put more money into savings, the lowest time-preference group) had BMI in 1992 about 0.4–0.5 units lower (≈0.08 SD) and 38–90% lower odds of obesity than dis-savers/non-savers, after adjustment for SES, education, race/ethnicity, sex, age, family background, cognitive ability and baseline BMI. The pattern is consistent with a causal role of time preference but is an observational association, not proof of causation.
